title: Ada Dayyala
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was Rav Yehudah’s student and attendant in Pumbedita. Tall for his generation, he reached Rav Yehudah’s shoulder, as in Niddah 28a. Perhaps he was called Dayyala because of his height, from the root dalah. [Bava Kamma 119a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Kamma.119a.5) has Rav Yehudah ruling for Ada Dayyala; [Rashi on Bava Kamma](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Bava_Kamma.119a.5.2) explains that he was an attendant hired to prepare food for feasts. In [Shabbat 148a](https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.148a.1), Rav Yehudah sends him to summon Rabbah bar bar Chana; [Rashi on Shabbat](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashi_on_Shabbat.148a.1.2) explains dayyala as an appointed official. [Berakhot 53b](https://www.sefaria.org/Berakhot.53b.11) has Rav Yehudah reciting the Saturday-night blessing at Ada Dayyala’s house.[^3]

notes.text: Hyman’s explanation of Dayyala through height is tentative. The cited Rashi explanations describe hired food-service work and an appointed attendant. רבב״ח is Rabbah bar bar Chana here.

Berakhot 53b directly names Ada Dayyala’s household. Consulted Vilna Rashi on Bava Kamma 119a reads “attendant of the Rabbis”; Hyman’s fuller hired feast-cook explanation and tentative height etymology remain his report. This short Rashi gloss does not establish the wording of another edition.

The linked Bava Kamma gloss has “attendant of the rabbis”; Hyman gives a fuller description of a hired feast attendant. The linked Shabbat gloss calls him an appointed official. Berakhot names his household, and Hyman’s proposed derivation from height remains tentative.
